claims.text: A blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at the site path /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/.
The post at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from AWS CDK to Pulumi.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS (CDK is AWS-only and cannot target other cloud providers).
Debugging AWS CDK deployments is difficult/frustrating because of the CloudFormation templates it generates.
Multi-cloud deployment with AWS CDK is nearly impossible.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience (faster deployments, multi-cloud flexibility).
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allows developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.

With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code acts as a code generator that produces an intermediary format (such as YAML or JSON) which is then executed to deploy the resources, so the code a developer writes is not the same as the code running during deployment.
The CDK/CloudFormation intermediary-format approach leads to difficulty debugging, lack of visibility into the deployment process, and challenges extending or customizing the deployment workflow.
The Pulumi docs have a CloudFormation comparison page with a section "What is AWS CloudFormation" at /docs/iac/comparisons/cloudformation/#what-is-aws-cloudformation.
The Pulumi docs have an AWS CDK comparison page with a section "What is AWS CDK" at /docs/iac/comparisons/aws-cdk/#what-is-aws-cdk that describes the AWS-centric nature of CDK.
The SST team expanded its focus beyond AWS to other cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure, and found the AWS-centric nature of CDK and CloudFormation a limitation.
Pulumi supports multi-cloud deployment across AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises; AWS CDK is AWS-only.
Pulumi offers "real-time debugging", whereas AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as programming languages.
Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower than Pulumi's because of CloudFormation; Pulumi is faster due to direct execution.
Pulumi provides clear deployment state visibility, whereas with AWS CDK it is hard to trace errors.
AWS CDK extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem, whereas Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows.
AWS CDK state management relies on a CloudFormation state file, whereas Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, whereas Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, rather than generating an intermediary format.
The SST team discovered Pulumi during the period when it was seeking a provider-agnostic solution beyond CDK/CloudFormation.
With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment, giving greater visibility into the deployment process and the ability to extend or customize it.
Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach lets SST's team work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.

SST's transition from CDK to Pulumi required re-implementing the higher-level components and abstractions built on top of CDK and handling edge cases and complex deployment scenarios, with the Pulumi-based version intended to match and improve on the CDK-based version.

The Founding Engineer at SST said: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
The image file sst-with-pulumi-infrastructure-as-code-deployments.png exists alongside the post.
The Pulumi Insights product page (/product/pulumi-insights/) describes improved visibility and debugging capabilities for Pulumi deployments.
In the CDK/CloudFormation approach, the intermediary format (CloudFormation templates) often obscures the underlying logic and makes problems harder to diagnose and resolve.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
The SST team used Pulumi's custom providers and dynamic components to integrate with cloud and on-premises services and implement complex deployment workflows.
With the CDK/CloudFormation approach, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired customization.
With Pulumi, the SST team was able to easily add support for new providers, letting users deploy across diverse environments.
With SST built on Pulumi, users can manage all of their infrastructure across multiple cloud providers and on-premises through a single, consistent interface without juggling multiple tools.
With SST built on Pulumi, SST users can write their infrastructure logic in the same programming languages they use for their application code.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy it across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
The SST team is exploring deeper integration with application frameworks, expanded provider support, improved deployment workflows, and enhanced observability and monitoring on top of Pulumi.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments documentation exists at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/ and covers advanced deployment workflows.
Pulumi's extensibility enables advanced deployment workflows with faster deployment times, better rollback capabilities, and more granular control over the deployment process.
The Pulumi Insights product page (/product/pulumi-insights/) describes better visibility into the deployment process and monitoring/observability capabilities.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, and the AWS guide is at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" at /resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi's resources page at /resources/#upcoming lists upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops.
The Pulumi signup page is at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure easy.
Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, in which constructs (components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation.
Once Ion is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service, SST Console.
The SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST relies primarily on SaaS revenue through its managed platform and potentially on supplemental income such as enterprise services and consulting.
Traditional infrastructure-as-code tools and approaches have often been geared more toward DevOps teams than application developers.
SST is a framework built to empower application developers, and its journey began with AWS CDK before it moved to Pulumi.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no Pulumi account (and no Pulumi Cloud dependency).
Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install because the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the Ion-based rewrite of the SST framework.
`sst deploy` uses no CDK and no CloudFormation.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
SST is still shipping releases, and the SST team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode.
The SST team has repeatedly said, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine (describing their own architecture this way).
SST is an open source TypeScript framework.
SST comes from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can build and deploy full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.

SST apps define infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components (functions, queues, buckets, static sites, etc.), and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
Ion (SST v3) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped.

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post "Moving away from CDK" says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs page "What is SST" says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."
Independent developers who have compared SST, Terraform, and Pulumi directly describe the same architecture (SST built on the Pulumi engine).

Gautier Blandin, in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis", writes: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka, in "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion", writes: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).

SST's `platform/package.json` lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The SST repository is now `anomalyco/sst` on GitHub, formerly `sst/sst`.
`sst deploy` reads `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations (dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking) within SST deployments.
Terraform-bridged providers (via Pulumi's Terraform bridge, github.com/pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) translate each Pulumi resource into cloud API calls.
Pulumi's engine provides the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing and maintaining their own.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API lets teams embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools, with the engine embedded in the same way as SST does (no account or Pulumi Cloud required).
The Pulumi provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
The page at /blog/any-terraform-provider/ exists and covers the Pulumi provider bridge; /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/ and /docs/iac/get-started/terraform/terraform-providers/ exist.
By embedding the Pulumi engine, SST gets a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers without building either from scratch.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Nitric's docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric deployment providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Defang's Pulumi provider README describes it as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
Nitric, Defang, and SST all expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
SST users are not Pulumi Cloud customers: SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket and SST doesn't require a Pulumi account.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.

Within an SST app, resources that lack a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly as Pulumi resources and deployed as part of the same app, because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week as of September 2026 (796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (star count) than SST itself.
SST's releases and download numbers show SST is not being abandoned.
The SST team's work on opencode has not changed SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine.
The team's attention to opencode has not changed SST's release cadence.
Anyone running SST is running Pulumi's engine, whether or not they have written any Pulumi code.
Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state.
Pulumi policy as code provides guardrails that a platform team can enforce centrally.
Pulumi components let teams share infrastructure patterns across a whole organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components can be adopted without leaving the Pulumi engine that SST already uses.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers that are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI and does not write Terraform state.
SST does not expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
SST is a strong fit for teams wanting an opinionated, full-stack application framework with infrastructure and code defined together.

Link targets exist: /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /blog/any-terraform-provider/, and /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/; the AWS CDK vs Pulumi post is titled "AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi" and tells the story of SST's move off CDK from SST's side.
